Jack Neton Section : Pokémon Type Balance by Generation¶

Final Project: Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Pokémon Type Balance¶

Jack Neton¶

November 2026¶

  • Main question: which Pokémon types are over- or under-represented, and has that changed across generations?

  • The notebook has three parts

    • Part 1, Summary Statistics: tables and numbers to see what the data looks like
    • Part 2, Exploratory Plots: quick, default-style charts to find patterns and problems
    • Part 3, Refined Charts: polished versions of the most useful plots, using the design principles from class

  • Questions raised in Parts 1 and 2 are answered further down, with a pointer to where

  • Data loading and cleaning follow Homework 7 (Week7_Homework7_PokemonTypes.ipynb), condensed here so this notebook runs on its own

In [ ]:
import pandas as pd
import altair as alt

alt.renderers.enable('default');

Data¶

Source: PokeAPI, data/v2/csv folder of the PokeAPI GitHub repository, https://github.com/PokeAPI/pokeapi/tree/master/data/v2/csv. Accessed November 10, 2026.

  • Same steps as Homework 7: base forms only (1,025 Pokémon), current types, type names merged in

  • Two main tables

    • mons: one row per Pokémon, with primary type (Type_1) and secondary type (Type_2, "None" if single type)
    • type_long: one row per Pokémon per type, so a dual-type Pokémon has 2 rows
In [ ]:
csv_url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/PokeAPI/pokeapi/master/data/v2/csv/'

pokemon_types = pd.read_csv(csv_url + 'pokemon_types.csv')
types = pd.read_csv(csv_url + 'types.csv')
pokemon = pd.read_csv(csv_url + 'pokemon.csv')
species = pd.read_csv(csv_url + 'pokemon_species.csv')
efficacy = pd.read_csv(csv_url + 'type_efficacy.csv')

# type ID -> name
type_names = types[['id', 'identifier', 'generation_id']].rename(columns={'id': 'type_id', 'identifier': 'Type', 'generation_id': 'Intro_Gen'})
type_names['Type'] = type_names['Type'].str.capitalize()

# base forms with generation
base_forms = pokemon[pokemon['is_default'] == 1][['id', 'identifier', 'species_id']].rename(columns={'id': 'pokemon_id', 'identifier': 'Name'})
base_forms = base_forms.merge(species[['id', 'generation_id']].rename(columns={'id': 'species_id', 'generation_id': 'Generation'}), on='species_id')
base_forms['Name'] = base_forms['Name'].str.capitalize()

# long table: one row per Pokémon per type
type_long = pokemon_types.merge(type_names[['type_id', 'Type']], on='type_id')
type_long = type_long.merge(base_forms[['pokemon_id', 'Name', 'Generation']], on='pokemon_id')
type_long['Slot'] = type_long['slot'].map({1: 'Primary type', 2: 'Secondary type'})

# wide table: one row per Pokémon
primary = type_long[type_long['slot'] == 1][['pokemon_id', 'Type']].rename(columns={'Type': 'Type_1'})
secondary = type_long[type_long['slot'] == 2][['pokemon_id', 'Type']].rename(columns={'Type': 'Type_2'})
mons = base_forms.merge(primary, on='pokemon_id').merge(secondary, on='pokemon_id', how='left')
mons['Type_2'] = mons['Type_2'].fillna('None')
mons['Dual_Type'] = mons['Type_2'] != 'None'

# types ordered from most to least common (used for every chart, so types sit in the same order throughout)
type_order = type_long['Type'].value_counts().index.tolist()

len(mons), len(type_long)
Out[ ]:
(1025, 1551)

1.2 Pokémon per type¶

type_counts = pd.DataFrame({
    'Primary': mons['Type_1'].value_counts(),

Comments

  • Counting both slots, the 18 types average 86 Pokémon each, with a median of 74.5
  • The mean is above the median because a few types are much larger: Water (154), Normal (131), Grass (127), Flying (109) and Psychic (102)
  • The most common type (Water) has 3.2 times as many Pokémon as the least common (Ice, 48)
  • Flying is the outlier in Pct_Secondary: 92% of Flying Pokémon have it as their second type. The next highest is Fairy at 55%
  • Bug (10%), Electric (14%) and Normal (10%) are almost never second types

1.4 Type share by generation¶

  • For each type and generation, the percent of that generation's Pokémon with the type (either slot)
  • A dual-type Pokémon counts for both of its types, so each generation's percentages add up to more than 100%
In [ ]:
# full grid of type x generation, so a type with no Pokémon in a generation shows 0 instead of a gap
type_gen_counts = type_long.groupby(['Type', 'Generation']).size()
gen_sizes = mons.groupby('Generation').size()
intro_gen = dict(zip(type_names['Type'], type_names['Intro_Gen']))

rows = []
for t in type_order:
    for g in range(1, 10):
        rows.append({'Type': t, 'Generation': g, 'Count': type_gen_counts.get((t, g), 0)})
type_gen = pd.DataFrame(rows)

type_gen['Pct'] = type_gen['Count'] / type_gen['Generation'].map(gen_sizes) * 100
type_gen['Intro_Gen'] = type_gen['Type'].map(intro_gen)
type_gen['Shade_End'] = type_gen['Intro_Gen'] - 0.5        # shading runs from 0.5 to just before the type was added

even_share = len(type_long) / len(mons) / 18 * 100          # share per type if all 18 were equal (types per Pokémon / 18)
len(type_gen), round(even_share, 1)

Comments

  • If all 18 types were equally common, each would be 8.4% of a generation (each Pokémon has 1.51 types on average, divided by 18)

  • Water (14.7% average), Normal (12.7%) and Grass (12.5%) are above that in almost every generation

  • Ice is below it in every generation (1.1% to 7.3%)

  • Standard deviation shows which types changed the most from generation to generation

    • Poison (5.9) and Fairy (5.6) changed the most, then Flying (4.3), Water (4.2) and Dragon (4.1)
    • Rock, Ice and Psychic barely changed (1.7–2.0)

  • Dark in Generation 1 is the only type-generation pair with 0 Pokémon, because Dark didn't exist yet

Questions

  • Which direction did the high-variation types move? (see Exploratory Plot 3 and Chart 2)

1.5 Type combinations¶

  • For dual-type Pokémon, I treat each pair as unordered (Grass / Poison is the same as Poison / Grass), since order doesn't matter in battle
In [ ]:
type_rank = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(type_order)}

duals = mons[mons['Dual_Type']].copy()
duals['Type_A'] = [a if type_rank[a] < type_rank[b] else b for a, b in zip(duals['Type_1'], duals['Type_2'])]   # more common type of the pair
duals['Type_B'] = [b if type_rank[a] < type_rank[b] else a for a, b in zip(duals['Type_1'], duals['Type_2'])]   # less common type
pair_counts = duals.groupby(['Type_A', 'Type_B']).size()

# every possible pair (153), including ones no Pokémon has
rows = []
for i, a in enumerate(type_order):
    for b in type_order[i + 1:]:
        rows.append({'Type_A': a, 'Type_B': b, 'Count': pair_counts.get((a, b), 0)})
pairs = pd.DataFrame(rows)

bins = [(0, 0, 'Never used'), (1, 1, '1'), (2, 3, '2–3'), (4, 6, '4–6'), (7, 12, '7–12'), (13, 100, '13 or more')]
pairs['Group'] = ''
for low, high, name in bins:
    pairs.loc[(pairs['Count'] >= low) & (pairs['Count'] <= high), 'Group'] = name

len(pairs), (pairs['Count'] == 0).sum()

1.6 Type matchups¶

  • From the matchup chart, for each type: how many types it resists (takes half or no damage from), how many it's weak to (takes double damage from), and a defensive score (resists − weaknesses)
In [ ]:
matchups = efficacy.merge(type_names[['type_id', 'Type']].rename(columns={'type_id': 'damage_type_id', 'Type': 'Attacking'}), on='damage_type_id')
matchups = matchups.merge(type_names[['type_id', 'Type']].rename(columns={'type_id': 'target_type_id', 'Type': 'Defending'}), on='target_type_id')

resists = matchups[matchups['damage_factor'] < 100].groupby('Defending').size()
weak_to = matchups[matchups['damage_factor'] == 200].groupby('Defending').size()

defense = pd.DataFrame({'Resists': resists, 'Weak_To': weak_to}).fillna(0).astype(int).reset_index(names='Type')
defense['Score'] = defense['Resists'] - defense['Weak_To']
defense['Pokemon'] = defense['Type'].map(type_long['Type'].value_counts())
defense['Label'] = defense['Type'] + ' (' + defense['Pokemon'].astype(str) + ')'      # e.g. "Water (154)"
defense['Side'] = ['Resists more than it\'s weak to' if s > 0 else 'Even or more weaknesses' for s in defense['Score']]

label_order = [f'{t} ({defense.set_index("Type").loc[t, "Pokemon"]})' for t in type_order]
defense.sort_values('Score', ascending=False)

Comments

  • A typical type resists 4 types and is weak to 3, for a median score of +0.5

  • Steel is the outlier: it resists 11 types, almost 3 times the median, for a score of +8

  • Ice is the lowest at −3 (resists only itself, weak to 4)

  • The correlation between number of Pokémon and defensive score is −0.09, and with types resisted −0.16

    • Close to zero, so how common a type is doesn't seem to be related to how strong it is defensively

Questions

  • Does a plot show any pattern the correlation misses? (see Exploratory Plot 6 and Chart 6)

Part 2: Exploratory Plots¶

  • Quick charts with Altair's default styling, to check the summary statistics and spot problems
  • No titles or design work yet; the comments note what each one shows and what to fix

Exploratory Plot 1: Primary type counts¶

  • Question: which types are most common if I only count each Pokémon's first type?
In [ ]:
alt.Chart(mons).mark_bar().encode(
    alt.X('count()'),
    alt.Y('Type_1:N', sort='-x')
)
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Water (134) and Normal (118) still lead

  • Flying drops to last, with 9 Pokémon, even though it's 4th when both slots are counted (Section 1.2)

  • Counting primary types only hides how Flying is used, so the refined chart should show both slots

    • Stacking primary and secondary in one bar keeps the total and the split together (see Chart 1)

Exploratory Plot 2: Pokémon per generation¶

  • Question: how different are the generation sizes?
In [ ]:
alt.Chart(mons).mark_bar().encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('count()')
)
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Generation 5 (156) is more than twice Generation 6 (72), and there's no trend over time
  • Confirms Section 1.1: any comparison across generations has to use percent of the generation, not counts
  • Not a chart for the final project, but it explains why the later charts use percentages

Exploratory Plot 3: Type × generation heatmap¶

  • Question: where are the big changes in the type mix?
  • Raw counts with the default color scheme
In [ ]:
alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_rect().encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('Type:N'),
    alt.Color('Count:Q')
)
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Poison and Water in Generation 1 are the darkest cells (33 and 32 Pokémon)

  • Generation 5's column looks darker overall, but that's because it's the largest generation (Exploratory Plot 2), not because its types are different

  • Hard to read for several reasons

    • Counts instead of percentages
    • Color alone for a quantitative value, so exact values can't be read (Week 6)
    • Types in alphabetical order, so nothing about the ranking is visible
    • Dark in Generation 1 is 0 because the type didn't exist, which looks the same as a type that was skipped

  • The refined version uses percentages, position instead of color, and one panel per type (see Chart 2)

    alt.Y('count()'),

Out[ ]:

  • The dual-type segment looks bigger in Generations 6, 7 and 9

  • Bar heights are the generation sizes again, so the segments are hard to compare

  • Generation 8 looks like Generations 1–5

Exploratory Plot 5: Spread of type shares within each generation¶

  • Question: is the type mix getting more even (Section 1.4)?
  • One tick per type in each generation
In [ ]:
alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_tick().encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q'),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Pct:Q']
)
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • The ticks are spread from 0% to 22% in Generation 1 and squeezed into 4–12% in Generation 8

  • Generation 6 spreads out again (Fairy at 18%), then Generations 8 and 9 are the tightest

  • So the trend toward a more even mix is real but not steady

  • Ticks overlap where several types have the same share, and the chart doesn't say which type is which without the tooltip

    • The refined version labels the top type in each generation (see Chart 7)

  • No pattern, which matches the near-zero correlation

  • The refined version is a diverging bar chart with one row per type, in the same order as Chart 1 (see Chart 6)

Part 3: Refined Charts¶

  • Seven charts based on Parts 1 and 2, using the design principles from class
  • Each one lists the question, variables, encodings, chart type and design choices

Design Setup¶

  • Theme (Week 7, accessibility: readable text, "utilize themes in Altair")

    • Larger fonts than the default (12–13 pt labels, 18 pt titles) in a plain sans-serif typeface
    • Neutral gray axes, grid lines and subtitles, so only the data has color (Week 6: neutral colors for non-data elements)
    • Titles in a dark navy that matches the Pokémon logo blue

  • Colors

    • Pokémon logo blue (#2A75BB) for single-series charts
    • Pokémon logo yellow (#FFCB05) isn't used for data marks: its contrast on white is 1.5:1, below the 3:1 that WCAG asks for graphics
    • The standard type colors used by the games' fan wikis, for charts where each type has its own panel or is picked from a menu
    • 10 of the 18 type colors (e.g. Electric yellow, Ice, Steel) are too light on white, so I darkened them just enough to reach 3:1 and kept the hue
    • 18 types is far past the ~8 nominal colors we can tell apart (Week 6), so type colors are never the only way to tell types apart: each chart also has a panel title, menu or text label
In [ ]:
# Pokémon logo colors and dark navy for text
POKE_BLUE = '#2A75BB'
POKE_BLUE_LIGHT = '#A9C8EA'       # lighter tint of the same blue, for an ordered second category

# project theme: larger readable text, neutral non-data elements
@alt.theme.register('pokemon', enable=True)
def pokemon_theme():
    return alt.theme.ThemeConfig({
        'config': {
            'font': 'Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif',
            'background': 'white',
            'view': {'stroke': None},
            'title': {'fontSize': 18, 'color': NAVY, 'anchor': 'start', 'subtitleFontSize': 13,
                      'subtitleColor': GRAY_TEXT, 'subtitlePadding': 6, 'offset': 14},
            'axis': {'labelFontSize': 12, 'titleFontSize': 13, 'labelColor': GRAY_TEXT, 'titleColor': GRAY_TEXT,
                     'titleFontWeight': 'normal', 'domainColor': '#9E9E9E', 'tickColor': '#9E9E9E', 'gridColor': '#E8E8E8'},
            'legend': {'labelFontSize': 12, 'titleFontSize': 13, 'labelColor': GRAY_TEXT, 'titleColor': GRAY_TEXT},
            'header': {'labelFontSize': 13, 'labelColor': NAVY, 'titleFontSize': 13},
            'text': {'fontSize': 12}
        }
    })

Chart 1: How common is each type?¶

  • Refines Exploratory Plot 1

  • Question: which types are most and least common, and how often is each one a Pokémon's first vs. second type?

  • Variables: Type, Slot (primary or secondary), count of Pokémon

  • Encodings

    • Type → y position, sorted by total
    • Count → bar length (x), starting at zero
    • Slot → color, two tints of the logo blue. The two slots are ordered (first, second), so a dark and light version of one hue fits better than two unrelated hues
    • Thin blue outline on every bar, so the light segment still has a visible edge on white
    • Total → text label at the end of each bar, so the reader doesn't have to add the two segments

  • Chart type: stacked horizontal bar chart

  • Design: legend at the top, close to where the reader starts; no vertical grid lines needed since every bar is labeled

In [ ]:
slot_order = {'Primary type': 1, 'Secondary type': 2}
type_long['Slot_Order'] = type_long['Slot'].map(slot_order)   # primary segment first

bars = alt.Chart(type_long).mark_bar(stroke=POKE_BLUE, strokeWidth=1).encode(   # blue outline keeps the light segment visible on white
    alt.X('count()', axis=alt.Axis(title='Number of Pokémon', grid=False)),
    alt.Y('Type:N', sort=type_order, axis=alt.Axis(title=None)),
    alt.Color('Slot:N', title=None,
              scale=alt.Scale(domain=['Primary type', 'Secondary type'], range=[POKE_BLUE, POKE_BLUE_LIGHT]),
              legend=alt.Legend(orient='top', direction='horizontal')),
    alt.Order('Slot_Order:Q'),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Slot:N', alt.Tooltip('count()', title='Pokémon')]
)

totals = alt.Chart(type_long).mark_text(align='left', dx=4, color=GRAY_TEXT).transform_aggregate(
    Total='count()',
    groupby=['Type']
).encode(
    alt.X('Total:Q'),
    alt.Y('Type:N', sort=type_order),
    text='Total:Q'
)

chart1 = (bars + totals).properties(
    width=480,
    height=420,
    title=alt.Title('Water is the most common type, and Flying is almost always a second type',
                    subtitle=['Number of Pokémon with each type, split by whether it is their first or second type',
                              '1,025 Pokémon (base forms), Generations 1–9 · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Stacked bar chart of the number of Pokémon with each of the 18 types. Water is most common with 154 Pokémon, '
                 'then Normal (131) and Grass (127); Ice is least common with 48. Flying has 109 Pokémon but only 9 have it as their '
                 'primary type; for the rest it is the secondary type.')
)
chart1
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Water (154), Normal (131) and Grass (127) lead; Ice (48) is last, about a third of Water
  • Flying stands out: almost the whole bar is the light secondary segment (100 of 109)
  • Bug, Fire, Electric and Normal are almost always primary types
  • Fairy, Dragon, Steel, Ghost, Poison and Ground are about half secondary

Still to improve

  • The light blue fill is only 1.7:1 against white, so I added a logo-blue outline to the bars (4.8:1) to keep the edge of each segment visible
  • Could highlight Flying, since it's the main point of the title

Chart 2: How has the type mix changed across generations?¶

  • Refines Exploratory Plot 3

  • Question: which types grew or shrank from Generation 1 to 9?

  • Variables: Type, Generation, percent of that generation's Pokémon with the type (computed in pandas, so generations of different sizes can be compared)

  • Encodings

    • Generation → x position, percent → y position (position is the most accurate channel)
    • Type → small multiple panel, in the same order as Chart 1
    • Type → line color, which only repeats the panel title, so color isn't needed to read the chart

  • Chart type: small multiples line chart (18 panels, shared y scale so panels can be compared)

  • Design

    • Gray shading for generations before a type existed (Dark and Steel added in Generation 2, Fairy in Generation 6)
    • Dashed reference line at 8.4%, the share each type would have if all 18 were equally common
In [ ]:
base = alt.Chart().encode(
    alt.X('Generation:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0.5, 9.5]),
          axis=alt.Axis(title='Generation', values=[1, 3, 5, 7, 9], grid=False))
)

not_yet = alt.Chart().mark_rect(color='#EFEFEF').transform_filter(
    'datum.Generation == 1 && datum.Intro_Gen > 1'           # one rectangle per type
).encode(
    alt.X('x0:Q'),
    alt.X2('Shade_End:Q')
).transform_calculate(
    x0='0.5'
)

even_line = alt.Chart().mark_rule(color='#9E9E9E', strokeDash=[4, 3]).encode(
    alt.Y('even:Q')
).transform_calculate(
    even=f'{even_share}'
)

lines = base.mark_line(strokeWidth=2.5, point=alt.OverlayMarkDef(size=25)).encode(
    alt.Y('Pct:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 25]),
          axis=alt.Axis(title=None, values=[0, 10, 20], labelExpr='datum.value + "%"')),   # % on the labels; full description in the subtitle
    alt.Color('Type:N', scale=alt.Scale(domain=list(type_colors.keys()), range=list(type_colors.values())), legend=None),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Generation:O', 'Count:Q', alt.Tooltip('Pct:Q', format='.1f', title='% of generation')]
)

chart2 = alt.layer(not_yet, even_line, lines, data=type_gen).properties(
    width=120,
    height=90
).facet(
    facet=alt.Facet('Type:N', sort=type_order, title=None),
    columns=6
).properties(
    title=alt.Title('Generation 1 leaned on Poison, Water and Flying; later generations added Dark, Ghost and Dragon',
                    subtitle=['Percent of each generation\'s Pokémon that have the type (primary or secondary)',
                              f'Dashed line = {even_share:.1f}%, the share if all 18 types were equally common · '
                              'Gray = generations before the type existed',
                              'Fairy Pokémon in Generations 1–5 were retyped to Fairy in Generation 6 · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Small multiples of 18 line charts, one per type, showing the percent of each generation\'s Pokémon with that type '
                 'from Generation 1 to 9. Poison is 22% of Generation 1 and stays under 10% afterward. Flying peaks at 19% in '
                 'Generation 2 and falls to 5% by Generation 9. Dark, Ghost and Dragon rise to over 10% of Generation 9. '
                 'Fairy peaks at 18% in Generation 6, the generation it was added.')
)
chart2
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Poison: 22% of Generation 1, then 10% or less in every later generation
  • Flying: rises to 19% in Generation 2 and falls to 5% by Generation 9, the clearest downward trend
  • Dark, Ghost and Dragon all finish above the dashed line in Generation 9 (11–12%)
  • Fairy jumps to 18% in Generation 6, the generation it was added, then settles back near the line
  • Most types stay within a few points of the dashed line in most generations, so the big imbalances are in a handful of types
  • The y-axis title was repeated on every row and overlapped, so I moved it to the subtitle and put % on the tick labels
  • The gray shading makes it clear that Dark's 0% in Generation 1 is because the type didn't exist, not because it was skipped

Still to improve

  • 18 panels is a lot for a presentation slide. For the final version I could keep the 4–6 types with the clearest trends and mention the rest in text
  • Panel titles are the only label; a short note on the strongest change in each highlighted panel would help in the report

Chart 3: Pick a type (interactive)¶

  • Same data and question as Chart 2, in one panel

  • Interaction (Week 7)

    • A dropdown menu (binding_select) picks the type to highlight. The menu works with a keyboard and has a large target, unlike clicking a thin line
    • The selected type is drawn in its type color; the other 17 stay as thin gray lines for context
    • Starts on Fairy, so the chart makes sense before anyone touches it. The interaction adds detail but isn't needed for the main point, which Chart 2 shows without it
    • Changes are immediate, and nothing moves on its own (no animation)

  • Encodings: generation → x, percent → y, selected type → color and line width

In [ ]:
pick_type = alt.selection_point(
    name='Pick',
    fields=['Type'],
    value=[{'Type': 'Fairy'}],                                    # starting selection
    bind=alt.binding_select(options=type_order, name='Type: ')
)

context = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_line(color='#D9D9D9', strokeWidth=1.2).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[1, 9]), axis=alt.Axis(title='Generation', values=list(range(1, 10)), format='d', grid=False)),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q', axis=alt.Axis(title='% of Pokémon in generation')),
    detail='Type:N'
).add_params(
    pick_type
)

highlight = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_line(strokeWidth=3.5, point=alt.OverlayMarkDef(size=60)).transform_filter(
    pick_type
).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:Q'),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q'),
    alt.Color('Type:N', scale=alt.Scale(domain=list(type_colors.keys()), range=list(type_colors.values())), legend=None),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Generation:O', 'Count:Q', alt.Tooltip('Pct:Q', format='.1f', title='% of generation')]
)

label = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_text(align='left', dx=8, fontSize=14, fontWeight='bold').transform_filter(
    pick_type
).transform_filter(
    'datum.Generation == 9'
).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:Q'),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q'),
    alt.Color('Type:N', scale=alt.Scale(domain=list(type_colors.keys()), range=list(type_colors.values())), legend=None),
    text='Type:N'
)

even_rule = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_rule(color='#9E9E9E', strokeDash=[4, 3]).encode(
    alt.Y('even:Q')
).transform_calculate(
    even=f'{even_share}'
)

chart3 = (context + even_rule + highlight + label).properties(
    width=520,
    height=300,
    title=alt.Title('How has each type\'s share changed?',
                    subtitle=['Pick a type from the menu below the chart · gray lines are the other 17 types',
                              f'Dashed line = {even_share:.1f}%, the share if all types were equal · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Interactive line chart of the percent of each generation\'s Pokémon with a selected type, Generations 1 to 9, '
                 'with the other 17 types in gray. A dropdown menu selects the type; Fairy is selected by default, peaking at 18% '
                 'in Generation 6.')
)
chart3
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • With Fairy selected, the Generation 6 peak stands well above the gray lines, and Generations 1–5 show the retyped Pokémon at 1–8%
  • Poison and Flying show the biggest early peaks; Water is highest in Generations 1–3 (18–21%) and drops to 10–15% after that
  • The gray lines show the spread: most values fall between about 2% and 15%

Still to improve

  • The tooltip only works on the highlighted line, which is what I want, but a viewer won't know tooltips exist unless told
  • On the website, the menu label could say what the chart is for ("Highlight a type")

Chart 4: Which type combinations exist?¶

  • Visualizes the pair counts from Section 1.5

  • Question: which pairs of types are common, and which have never been used?

  • Variables: the two types of each dual-type Pokémon (526 Pokémon), as an unordered pair, and the count per pair

  • Order doesn't matter in battle, so "Normal / Flying" and "Flying / Normal" are combined, and each pair appears once (upper triangle)

  • Encodings

    • Type A → x, Type B → y, both in the Chart 1 order (most to least common)
    • Count → color, binned into 5 ordered groups with a single-hue blue scheme (Week 6: bin quantitative data shown with color, use a sequential scheme for unsigned data)
    • Count → text label in each cell, so the exact value doesn't depend on color
    • Never-used pairs → light gray, a neutral color outside the blue scale

  • Chart type: heatmap (triangular matrix)

In [ ]:
group_names = [name for low, high, name in bins]
group_colors = ['#EDEDED', '#DCE8F5', '#A9C8EA', '#6A9FD6', POKE_BLUE, NAVY]

cells_ = alt.Chart(pairs).mark_rect(stroke='white', strokeWidth=1.5).encode(
    alt.X('Type_A:N', sort=type_order[:-1], axis=alt.Axis(title=None, orient='top', labelAngle=-45, domain=False, ticks=False)),
    alt.Y('Type_B:N', sort=type_order[1:], axis=alt.Axis(title=None, domain=False, ticks=False)),
    alt.Color('Group:N', title='Pokémon with the pair',
              scale=alt.Scale(domain=group_names, range=group_colors),
              legend=alt.Legend(orient='right')),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip('Type_A:N', title='Type'), alt.Tooltip('Type_B:N', title='Type'), alt.Tooltip('Count:Q', title='Pokémon')]
)

counts_text = alt.Chart(pairs).mark_text(fontSize=11).transform_filter(
    'datum.Count > 0'
).encode(
    alt.X('Type_A:N', sort=type_order[:-1]),
    alt.Y('Type_B:N', sort=type_order[1:]),
    text='Count:Q',
    color=alt.condition('datum.Count >= 7', alt.value('white'), alt.value(NAVY))    # white text on the two darkest groups
)

chart4 = (cells_ + counts_text).properties(
    width=17 * 28,
    height=17 * 28,
    title=alt.Title('136 of 153 possible type pairs exist, and Normal / Flying is far ahead of the rest',
                    subtitle=['Number of dual-type Pokémon with each pair of types (order doesn\'t matter) · 526 Pokémon',
                              'Gray = no Pokémon has ever had the pair · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Triangular heatmap of how many Pokémon have each pair of types. Normal / Flying is the most common pair with 27 '
                 'Pokémon, followed by Grass / Poison (14) and Bug / Flying (13). 17 of 153 possible pairs have never been used, '
                 'including Fire / Fairy, Dragon / Fairy, Normal / Ghost and Steel / Ice.')
)
chart4
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Normal / Flying (27) is about twice the next pair, Grass / Poison (14), then Bug / Flying (13)
  • Flying is in 3 of the 5 most common pairs (with Normal, Bug and Water), which matches Chart 1: Flying is mostly added as a second type
  • 17 pairs have never been used, and Normal and Ice account for 9 of them (e.g. Normal / Ghost, Normal / Steel, Fire / Ice, Steel / Ice)
  • Fairy has 4 missing pairs (Fire, Ground, Dragon, Ice), probably because it's newer
  • Most used pairs have only 1–3 Pokémon, so a few common pairs make up a large share of dual types

Still to improve

  • The lightest blue group (1) and the gray "never used" cells are close in color; the number in each blue cell is what separates them, so the chart relies on the labels there
  • Could be split by early (Gen 1–4) vs. recent (Gen 5–9) generations to see whether newer games use more unusual pairs

Chart 5: Are newer Pokémon more often dual-type?¶

  • Refines Exploratory Plot 4

  • Question: has the share of Pokémon with two types changed by generation?

  • Variables: Generation, percent of the generation with a secondary type

  • Encodings: generation → x (ordered), percent → bar height starting at zero, percent → text label above each bar

  • Chart type: vertical bar chart, one color (logo blue), since generation is already on the x-axis

  • Design: dashed reference line at the all-generation average (51%), explained in the subtitle; value labels inside the top of each bar so they don't collide with the line

In [ ]:
dual_bars = alt.Chart(dual_by_gen).mark_bar(color=POKE_BLUE, size=36).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O', axis=alt.Axis(title='Generation', labelAngle=0)),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 80]), axis=alt.Axis(title='% of Pokémon with two types', values=[0, 20, 40, 60, 80])),
    tooltip=['Generation:O', alt.Tooltip('Pct:Q', format='.0f', title='% dual-type')]
)

dual_labels = dual_bars.mark_text(baseline='top', dy=6, color='white', fontWeight='bold').encode(   # inside the top of each bar, clear of the average line
    text=alt.Text('Pct:Q', format='.0f')
)

avg_rule = alt.Chart(dual_by_gen).mark_rule(color='#757575', strokeDash=[4, 3]).encode(
    alt.Y('avg:Q')
).transform_calculate(
    avg=f'{overall_dual}'
)

chart5 = (dual_bars + avg_rule + dual_labels).properties(
    width=440,
    height=280,
    title=alt.Title('Newer generations have more dual-type Pokémon, except Generation 8',
                    subtitle=[f'Percent of each generation\'s Pokémon that have two types · dashed line = all generations ({overall_dual:.0f}%) · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Bar chart of the percent of Pokémon with two types in each generation: 44% in Generation 1, 49% in Generations 2 '
                 'and 3, 50% in 4, 47% in 5, 57% in 6, 63% in 7, 46% in 8 and 64% in 9. The average across all generations is 51%.')
)
chart5
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • Generations 1–5 are all below the 51% average (44–50%)
  • Generations 6, 7 and 9 are well above it (57–64%)
  • Generation 8 (46%) breaks the pattern, dropping back to Generation 1–5 levels
  • My first version had the labels above the bars and a text label on the average line, and they ran into each other, so the labels are now inside the bars and the line is explained in the subtitle

Still to improve

  • Generation 1–5 bars are all close to 50%, so the white labels sit right at the dashed line; a lighter dash color could help
  • The 20-point rise from Generation 1 to 9 is clear, but it isn't steady, so the title shouldn't call it a trend

Chart 6: Are common types weaker?¶

  • Refines Exploratory Plot 6

  • Question: is how common a type is related to how strong it is defensively?

  • Variables: defensive score and number of Pokémon for each type (Section 1.6)

  • Encodings

    • Type → y position, in the Chart 1 order (most to least common), so the reader can see whether score follows commonness
    • Defensive score → bar length from zero (diverging)
    • Above or below zero → color: logo blue for positive and gray for negative (Week 6: diverging data, highlight what matters). The sign is also in the text label, so color isn't required

  • Chart type: diverging horizontal bar chart, instead of the scatter plot in Exploratory Plot 6, where several types landed on the same points

In [ ]:
def_bars = alt.Chart(defense).mark_bar(size=18).encode(
    alt.X('Score:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[-4, 9]),
          axis=alt.Axis(title='Defensive score (types resisted − types weak to)', values=list(range(-4, 10, 2)))),
    alt.Y('Label:N', sort=label_order, axis=alt.Axis(title='Type (number of Pokémon), most to least common', grid=False)),
    alt.Color('Side:N', title=None,
              scale=alt.Scale(domain=['Resists more than it\'s weak to', 'Even or more weaknesses'], range=[POKE_BLUE, '#A6A6A6']),
              legend=alt.Legend(orient='top')),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Pokemon:Q', 'Resists:Q', 'Weak_To:Q', 'Score:Q']
)

def_text = alt.Chart(defense).mark_text(color=GRAY_TEXT).transform_calculate(
    txt='datum.Score > 0 ? "+" + datum.Score : "" + datum.Score',
    pos='datum.Score >= 0 ? datum.Score + 0.35 : datum.Score - 0.35'      # just past the end of the bar
).encode(
    alt.X('pos:Q'),
    alt.Y('Label:N', sort=label_order),
    text='txt:N'
)

zero_line = alt.Chart(defense).mark_rule(color='#757575').encode(x=alt.datum(0))

chart6 = (def_bars + zero_line + def_text).properties(
    width=440,
    height=430,
    title=alt.Title('Defensive strength doesn\'t follow how common a type is; Steel is far ahead',
                    subtitle=['Types each type resists minus types it is weak to, from the current matchup chart',
                              'Types listed from most to least common (Chart 1) · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Diverging bar chart of each type\'s defensive score, the number of types it resists minus the number it is weak to, '
                 'with types listed from most to least common. Steel has the highest score, +8, and Ice the lowest, −3. There is no '
                 'clear pattern between how common a type is and its score: Water, the most common type, is +2, and Ice, the least '
                 'common, is −3.')
)
chart6
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • No clear relationship: positive and negative scores are spread through the whole list
  • Steel (+8) is far ahead, resisting 11 types and weak to 3
  • The two least common types are opposites: Fairy is +2, Ice is −3 (the lowest)
  • Grass, Rock and Psychic are below zero; Normal is 0, with one immunity (Ghost) and one weakness (Fighting)
  • This only covers defense. A type that's weak defensively can still be strong on offense (e.g. Ice hits 4 types for double damage)

Still to improve

  • Add offense as a second panel with the same y order, so the reader can compare both sides of type strength
  • The score treats an immunity the same as a resistance, which understates types like Ghost and Steel

Chart 7: Is the type mix getting more even?¶

  • Refines Exploratory Plot 5

  • Question: are later generations spread more evenly across the 18 types?

  • Variables: Generation, each type's percent of the generation (Section 1.4), the highest and lowest share per generation

  • Encodings

    • Generation → x, percent → y (position)
    • Each type → one gray dot, so the spread of the dots shows how even the mix is
    • A vertical line from the lowest to the highest share in each generation, so the range is visible at a glance
    • The most common type in each generation → logo-blue dot with a text label, so the reader knows what drives the top of the range

  • Chart type: strip plot with range lines

  • Design: same dashed 8.4% "even share" line as Charts 2 and 3; gray for context, one highlight color

In [ ]:
# most common type(s) in each generation, for labels (two types tie in Generations 7 and 8)
top_rows = []
for g in range(1, 10):
    gen_rows = type_gen[type_gen['Generation'] == g]
    top = gen_rows[gen_rows['Pct'] == gen_rows['Pct'].max()]
    top_rows.append({'Generation': g, 'Pct': top['Pct'].iloc[0], 'Top_Type': ' / '.join(top['Type'])})
top_types = pd.DataFrame(top_rows)
top_types
Out[ ]:
Generation Pct Top_Type
0 1 21.854305 Poison
1 2 19.000000 Flying
2 3 20.740741 Water
3 4 15.887850 Normal
4 5 12.820513 Grass
5 6 18.055556 Fairy
6 7 14.772727 Water / Grass
7 8 11.458333 Water / Dragon
8 9 16.666667 Grass
In [ ]:
type_dots = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_circle(size=55, color='#A6A6A6', opacity=0.7).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O', axis=alt.Axis(title='Generation', labelAngle=0)),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q', scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, 25]),
          axis=alt.Axis(title=None, values=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25], labelExpr='datum.value + "%"')),
    tooltip=['Type:N', 'Generation:O', 'Count:Q', alt.Tooltip('Pct:Q', format='.1f', title='% of generation')]
)

ranges = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_rule(color='#BDBDBD', strokeWidth=2).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('min(Pct):Q'),
    alt.Y2('max(Pct):Q')
)

top_dots = alt.Chart(top_types).mark_circle(size=90, color=POKE_BLUE, opacity=1).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q'),
    tooltip=[alt.Tooltip('Top_Type:N', title='Most common type'), alt.Tooltip('Pct:Q', format='.1f', title='% of generation')]
)

top_labels = alt.Chart(top_types).mark_text(baseline='bottom', dy=-9, color=NAVY, fontSize=12).encode(
    alt.X('Generation:O'),
    alt.Y('Pct:Q'),
    text='Top_Type:N'
)

even_rule7 = alt.Chart(type_gen).mark_rule(color='#9E9E9E', strokeDash=[4, 3]).encode(
    alt.Y('even:Q')
).transform_calculate(
    even=f'{even_share}'
)

chart7 = (ranges + even_rule7 + type_dots + top_dots + top_labels).properties(
    width=520,
    height=320,
    title=alt.Title('The type mix has become more even over time',
                    subtitle=['Generation 1\'s types ranged from 0% to 22% of its Pokémon; Generation 8\'s from 4% to 12%',
                              'Percent of each generation\'s Pokémon with each type · one dot per type, most common type in blue',
                              f'Dashed line = {even_share:.1f}%, the share if all 18 types were equal · Source: PokeAPI']),
    description=('Strip plot of the percent of each generation\'s Pokémon with each of the 18 types, with a line showing the range. '
                 'Generation 1 ranges from 0% (Dark) to 22% (Poison). The range narrows in later generations, to 4–12% in Generation 8 '
                 'and 5–17% in Generation 9. The most common type is Poison in Generation 1, Flying in 2, Water in 3, Normal in 4, '
                 'Grass in 5, Fairy in 6, Grass and Water (tied) in 7, Dragon and Water (tied) in 8 and Grass in 9.')
)
chart7
Out[ ]:

Comments

  • The range narrows from 22 points in Generation 1 to 7 points in Generation 8
  • Generations 1–3 each had one type at about 19–22% (Poison, Flying, Water); no type has passed 17% since Generation 6
  • Generation 6 is the exception: Fairy's debut pushes it to 18%
  • The most common type changes almost every generation. Counting ties, Grass leads 3 times (Generations 5, 7 and 9) and so does Water (3, 7 and 8)
  • The lowest dots are mostly types that were new or rare at the time (Dark, Steel, Dragon and Ghost early on, Fairy before Generation 6)

Still to improve

  • The dots overlap where several types share the same percent; a little horizontal jitter would separate them
  • Could add the standard deviation from Section 1.4 as a small line chart underneath, though the range lines may be enough

Summary¶

  • What the EDA shows

    • Types aren't balanced overall: Water has 3.2 times as many Pokémon as Ice, and Flying is almost only a second type (Section 1.2, Chart 1)
    • The type mix has become more even over time. The spread of type shares within a generation fell from 6.3 points (Generation 1) to 2.2–2.8 (Generations 8–9) (Section 1.4, Chart 7)
    • The biggest individual changes are Poison and Flying falling after Generations 1–2, Dark, Ghost and Dragon rising, and Fairy's jump in Generation 6 (Chart 2)
    • Newer generations have more dual-type Pokémon, except Generation 8 (Chart 5)
    • A few pairs (Normal / Flying, Grass / Poison, Bug / Flying) are common and 17 have never been used (Chart 4)
    • How common a type is isn't related to its defensive strength (correlation −0.09, Chart 6)

  • Strongest candidates for the final report: Charts 1, 2, 4 and 7. Chart 3 is the interactive version of Chart 2 for the website. Charts 5 and 6 are secondary findings

  • Principles applied from class

    • Position and length for every main comparison; color only to label, group or highlight (Week 6)
    • Neutral grays for axes, grid lines and context, so the data stands out (Week 6)
    • No more than 6 colors in any one chart with a legend; type colors only where a panel title, menu or text label also identifies the type (Week 6)
    • Sequential single-hue scheme with binned values and text labels for the heatmap (Week 6)
    • Line and bar colors checked for at least 3:1 contrast on white; the lightest heatmap cells and the light bar segment rely on labels and outlines instead (Week 7, accessibility)
    • Alt-text in every chart's description property, larger fonts through a theme, a keyboard-friendly menu and no animation (Week 7)

  • To agree on as a group: the theme and color settings in Part 3, so everyone's charts match
